title: Users choose to engage with more partisan news than they are exposed to on Google Search
screen_reason: Two-wave digital-trace study (2018, 2020) of US participants running a browser extension that captured what they SAW on Google Search (SERP HTML snapshots), what they FOLLOWED from those results, and what they visited overall (Browser History). Reports quantitative shares with denominators of unreliable-news domains in exposure, follows and overall engagement (Table S7), and reports the percentage of participants who account for 90% of all unreliable news in each data type (concentration). Unreliable news is defined by two domain-reliability lists (NewsGuard <60; Grinberg et al. 2019 black/red/orange), i.e. source-level ground truth. EXPOSURE and CONCENTRATION estimates present.

estimates.date: October through December 2018
estimates.measure_type: % of all URLs seen in participants' Google Search results that came from unreliable news domains (participant-level average)
estimates.value_raw: 0.12% (Table S7, row '2018 Google Search Exposure / Google SERPs', URLs > Unreliable column)
estimates.denominator: all URLs appearing in the Google Search result pages the average participant was exposed to (1,245,155 URLs from 102,114 searches by 275 participants, 2018 wave; Table S4)
estimates.definition: URL whose second-level domain appears on the study's unreliable-news domain list (NewsGuard reliability score below 60, or one of the 490 black/red/orange domains of Grinberg et al. 2019)
estimates.misinfo_def: "We classified 2,962 web domains as unreliable if they appeared in either of two carefully constructed lists" - NewsGuard score <60 and the Grinberg et al. (2019) black/red/orange fake-news domain list
estimates.page_loc: Supplementary Table S7 (row: 2018, Google Search Exposure, Google SERPs)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level reliability lists, no coding by the authors: NewsGuard's journalist-rated scores (2,534 domains scored below the NewsGuard threshold of 60) plus the 490 domains manually coded black/red/orange by Grinberg et al. (2019); 2,962 unreliable domains in total. No reliability statistic reported (lists adopted as given).
estimates.moderator_quote: We classified 2,962 web domains as unreliable if they appeared in either of two carefully constructed lists [45, 48].
estimates.notes: Participant-level average (mean of individual participants' proportions), not the pooled item share; the pooled share would be 3,932/1,245,155. denom_selection=curated only because the extension captured the first search results page only ("we only collected the first page of search results"), which is a rank-truncated view; the capture is otherwise ecological (what actually appeared on participants' screens), so an adjudicator may prefer denom_selection="".

estimates.date: October through December 2018
estimates.measure_type: % of the NEWS URLs seen in participants' Google Search results that came from unreliable news domains (participant-level average)
estimates.value_raw: 2.05% (Table S7, row '2018 Google Search Exposure / Google SERPs', URLs > Unreliable (News) column); main text: "unreliable news was the least prevalent in their exposure (2.05% in 2018, 0.72% in 2020)"
estimates.denominator: news-domain URLs appearing in the Google Search result pages the average participant was exposed to (215,699 news URLs out of 1,245,155 SERP URLs, 275 participants, 2018 wave; Table S4)
estimates.definition: News URL whose second-level domain appears on the study's unreliable-news domain list (NewsGuard score <60, or Grinberg et al. 2019 black/red/orange)
estimates.misinfo_def: "We classified 2,962 web domains as unreliable if they appeared in either of two carefully constructed lists" - NewsGuard score <60 and the Grinberg et al. (2019) black/red/orange fake-news domain list
estimates.page_loc: Supplementary Table S7 (row: 2018, Google Search Exposure, Google SERPs); value also stated in Results
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level reliability lists, no coding by the authors: NewsGuard (score <60; 2,534 domains) plus the 490 black/red/orange domains of Grinberg et al. (2019); 2,962 unreliable domains. No reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Here we report the overall percentage of the URLs that came from news and unreliable news domains (using the total URL count as the denominator), as well as the percentage of news that came from unreliable domains (using the total news domain count as the denominator), for the average participant.
estimates.notes: Same numerator as the 0.12% row, narrower denominator (news URLs only), hence definition_variant=true - do not pool with the all-URL row. The main text says of this number "For exposure, this percentage represents the fraction of SERPs that contained at least one unreliable news domain", which contradicts Table S7, where 2.05% sits in the URL-level 'Unreliable (News)' column and the SERP-level figures are 2.46% and 4.79%. Coded per the table caption, which is explicit.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) TITLE/VERSION: the text file is the arXiv version of this study, titled 'Engagement Outweighs Exposure to Partisan and Unreliable News within Google Search' (Robertson, Green, Ruck, Ognyanova, Wilson, Lazer), not the manifest title 'Users choose to engage with more partisan news than they are exposed to on Google Search'. Same authors, same two-wave design, same measures, so I treated it as the paper and coded text_status=ok - but an adjudicator should know the values come from the preprint and may have been revised in the published version. (2) The main text says of 2.05%/0.72% 'For exposure, this percentage represents the fraction of SERPs that contained at least one unreliable news domain', which contradicts Table S7, where those values sit in the URL-level 'Unreliable (News)' column and the SERP-level values are 2.46%/1.18% (any unreliable domain) and 4.79%/2.18% (of searches returning news). I coded per the Table S7 caption; if the main text is right, the 2.05/0.72 rows and the 2.46/1.18 rows would swap meanings. (3) NOT extracted: partisan-news measures (rank-weighted mean audience-bias scores, and the partisan gaps of 0.062/0.037/0.106/0.096/0.206/0.134) - these are mean partisanship scores, not shares of misinformation. (4) NOT extracted: news prevalence (14.31%/14.71% of exposure URLs, 7.11%/3.24% of engagement URLs) - a share of news, not of misinformation. (5) NOT extracted: Gini coefficients for unreliable news (exposure 0.771/0.811, follows 0.801/0.939, engagement 0.915/0.893) - concentration but with no group%/share% pair, so unusable under R1. (6) NOT extracted as separate rows: the alternative engagement instruments (2018 Google History: 10.91% news, 0.54% unreliable, 3.64% unreliable-of-news; 2020 Tab Activity: 4.36%, 0.05%, 0.99%) - same construct measured with a second log, recorded here rather than duplicated as rows. (7) NOT extracted: the 'Unreliable (News)' Searches column (4.79% in 2018, 2.18% in 2020), which is a ratio of two SERP-level shares rather than a clean prevalence. (8) NOT extracted: regression coefficients, and subgroup (7-point PID, age) differences shown only in figures without printed values. (9) Sample-count discrepancy: the main text reports exposure for 276 participants and 105,327 SERPs in 2018 and 227,659 SERPs / 459 participants in 2020, whereas Table S4 reports 275 participants / 102,114 searches and 459 / 226,035; I used the Table S4 counts for n. (10) Waves kept as separate estimates because the 2018 (YouGov, strong-partisan oversample) and 2020 (PureSpectrum COVID States opt-in) samples are different people, not repeated measures of one panel.

rob.design: Two waves of opt-in browser-extension digital-trace collection in the US. 2018: YouGov survey fielded 18-24 October 2018 with an oversample of strong partisans, 11.5% of 3,106 survey respondents installed the extension; 2020: PureSpectrum quota sample within the COVID States Project (June 2020-January 2021), 0.4% of 189,711 survey respondents installed the extension - so both trace samples are self-selected and non-representative (2018: 36.7% strong Democrats, 27.5% strong Republicans; desktop only, first search-results page only). Exposure = HTML snapshots of Google SERPs; follows = Google History (2018) / Tab Activity (2020); overall engagement = Browser History; participants with a participation window under 10 days were dropped (2018: 30 SERP, 5 Google History, 7 Browser History participants; 2020: 182, 234, 32). Misinformation is coded at domain level from two external lists (NewsGuard score <60; Grinberg et al. 2019 black/red/orange), so no author coding and no inter-coder reliability statistic; the authors note the domain-level limitation explicitly. Group differences tested with Kruskal-Wallis and Spearman correlations; regressions are OLS (partisanship) and negative binomial (unreliable counts). Data cannot be shared (IRB).
